claims.claim: Stable item names make the prospective editor’s revision more accurate than explicit original-position wording.
Delete the first item, then tag the second always tags the item that was second before deletion.
Swapping deletion and tagging preserves the result of every positional edit pair.
A stable ID remains a unique selector when two live items share that ID.
Deleting A and tagging B fail to commute even when IDs are unique, A differs from B, and both are present.
Reordering items before an edit preserves the meaning of every current-position selector.
A deleted item can be selected as a live item without a tombstone or history mechanism.
Visible text is a unique item identity even when two items have identical text.
An ordinal retains its referent after insertion before that ordinal.
Every deletion instruction can be safely repeated with the same positional arguments.
A stable item ID proves that the item’s contents have not changed.
A patch’s final list alone proves that only the requested operations occurred.
The phrase move it supplies a unique referent after mentioning A and B without a binding rule.
A numbered display tells the editor whether its indices are zero-based or one-based without a convention.
An ID-based patch applies to every document version containing the same IDs.
Checking selectors after performing the first destructive edit is equivalent to checking all selectors before it.
Two selectors naming the same live item always denote two independent operations.
A text-only after-state diff uniquely identifies the item changed when duplicate text records exchange positions.
